name: Generative AI
oneBreath: AI that makes new things — text, images, code — instead of only sorting or labeling what already exists.
does: Write or create from a request
doesNot: Not every kind of AI
Not magic — it predicts what usually comes next
analogy: A very fluent autocomplete for words and ideas.
example: Chatbots, image makers, coding helpers.

name: Foundations
oneBreath: The basic building blocks: how these systems read text and pick what to say next.
does: Explain the small pieces behind chat AI
doesNot: Not a full math course
Not how to train a model from scratch

name: Models
oneBreath: How the big chat brains are built, trained, and taught to follow instructions.
doesNot: Not a guide to computer chips
Not a list of every brand name

name: Talking to models
oneBreath: How you write requests so the AI understands what you want — and what to avoid.
does: Show patterns like examples and step-by-step
doesNot: Not changing the model’s core training
Not a guarantee of perfect answers

name: Giving models knowledge
oneBreath: Ways to give the AI fresh or private facts so it doesn’t only rely on what it memorized.
doesNot: Not the same as retraining the whole model
Not perfect truth every time

name: Building with models
oneBreath: Turning a chat model into something that can take steps, use apps, and finish real jobs.
does: Connect AI to actions and tools
doesNot: Not always needed for a simple Q&A
Not the same as a real human worker

name: Trust & quality
oneBreath: Checking whether the AI is safe, accurate, fast enough, and worth the cost.
doesNot: Not a single perfect score
Not only “does it feel right?”

name: Token
oneBreath: A tiny piece of text the AI reads and writes — often part of a word, not always a whole word.
doesNot: Not always one full word
Not the same as meaning or memory
analogy: LEGO bricks that build a sentence.
example: “Chatbot” might be one piece or two.

name: Embedding
oneBreath: A way to turn text into a list of numbers so similar meanings sit near each other.
doesNot: Not human-readable text
Not a full answer by itself

nextStep.label: See how much it can read at once

analogy: A map where similar ideas live on nearby streets.
example: “Doctor” and “physician” land close on that map.

name: Context window
oneBreath: How much text the AI can see at once in this chat — like a limited desk size.
does: Hold the conversation and pasted files for a while
doesNot: Not infinite memory of everything forever
Not the same as saving facts across days

nextStep.label: See how it picks the next word

analogy: A whiteboard that only fits so many notes.
example: A long PDF may not fit in one go.

name: Probability / next-token
oneBreath: The AI writes by repeatedly guessing the most likely next little piece of text.
does: Explain why answers can change each time
doesNot: Not a guarantee the answer is true
Not careful planning like a person
analogy: A game of “what word comes next?”
example: Same question, two slightly different replies.

name: Temperature
oneBreath: A creativity dial: low = safer and more repetitive; high = more surprising wording.
does: Change how random the wording feels
Trade fun ideas vs steady answers
doesNot: Not a measure of how smart the AI is
Not a switch for truthfulness
analogy: Turning the spice up or down on a recipe.
example: Brainstorming high; careful code lower.

name: LLM
oneBreath: A large language model: software trained on lots of text to continue writing in a helpful way.
doesNot: Not a search engine by itself
Not always up to date on brand-new facts

nextStep.label: See the design behind chat models

analogy: A student who read a huge library and now finishes your sentences.
example: The engine behind most chat assistants.

name: Transformer
oneBreath: The popular design pattern behind modern chat AIs — good at relating words across a sentence.
does: Handle long-ish text better than older designs
doesNot: Not a power-line transformer
Not the only possible AI design

nextStep.label: See how it focuses on words

analogy: A seating chart that shows who should listen to whom in a room.
example: The “T” in many model names you see online.

name: Attention
oneBreath: A trick that lets the AI focus on the most useful earlier words when writing the next one.
does: Connect related words in a sentence
doesNot: Not human focus or mindfulness
Not a button in an app
analogy: Highlighting the important lines in a paragraph.
example: Linking “it” back to the right noun.

name: Pretraining
oneBreath: The long first training stage: read huge amounts of text to learn language patterns.
does: Teach grammar, facts, and style in bulk
Create the base model before special tuning
doesNot: Not the final “be a helpful assistant” training
Not something you do in a normal chat
analogy: Years of general school before a job.
example: Training on books, websites, and code at huge scale.

name: Fine-tuning
oneBreath: Extra training on a smaller, focused set of examples so the model gets better at one job.
does: Specialize for a domain or style
Change behavior more deeply than a prompt
doesNot: Not the same as pasting docs into the chat
Not free or instant — it needs data and compute

nextStep.label: See how it learns to follow asks

analogy: Job training after general school.
example: Teaching a model your company’s support tone.

name: Instruction tuning
oneBreath: Training that teaches the model to follow directions like “summarize this” or “be brief.”
does: Make models better at obeying asks
Turn a raw text predictor into an assistant
doesNot: Not teaching brand-new world facts alone
Not a substitute for safety checks
analogy: Practice drills: “when asked X, answer like Y.”
example: Chat models that wait for your request instead of rambling.

name: Alignment (RLHF / preference)
oneBreath: Shaping the model so it prefers helpful, honest, harmless answers — closer to what people want.
doesNot: Not perfect safety
Not the same as looking up fresh documents
analogy: Coaching that rewards good behavior.
example: Humans ranking which reply feels better (often called RLHF).

name: Prompt
oneBreath: The text you type (or send) that tells the AI what to do.
does: Steer the answer with clear goals
doesNot: Not the model’s permanent memory
Not a magic spell — clarity still matters
analogy: A brief you hand to a contractor.
example: “Explain this error in simple words.”

name: System vs user message
oneBreath: Two roles in a chat: system = standing rules; user = your request this turn.
does: Set ongoing behavior with system text
Keep your ask separate from the rules
doesNot: Not always visible in every consumer app
Not a guarantee users can’t trick the rules
analogy: Employee handbook (system) vs today’s ticket (user).
example: “You are a concise tutor” vs “Explain RAG.”

name: Few-shot
oneBreath: Showing a few examples in your ask so the AI copies the pattern you want.
doesNot: Not the same as full fine-tuning
Not free if examples eat your length limit
analogy: Show two sample answers, then ask for a third.
example: Two labeled emails, then “label this one.”

name: Chain-of-thought
oneBreath: Asking the AI to reason step by step before the final answer.
does: Make the path easier to check
doesNot: Not always needed for simple facts
Not a proof the reasoning is correct
analogy: Showing your work on a math test.
example: “Think step by step, then give the total.”

name: Structured output
oneBreath: Making the AI answer in a fixed shape — like JSON fields — so software can use it reliably.
does: Feed other apps without messy parsing
doesNot: Not always prettier for humans to read
Not a promise every field is true
analogy: Filling a form instead of writing an essay.
example: Return {name, price, inStock} for a product.

name: Prompt injection
oneBreath: A trick where hidden or pasted text tries to make the AI ignore its real instructions.
does: Risk tools or data if the AI obeys
doesNot: Not the same as breaking into the model’s files
Not fixed by turning temperature down
analogy: A sticky note on a recipe: “ignore the chef.”
example: A webpage telling a browsing bot to email secrets.
changing: As bots read more untrusted pages, this becomes a day-one design worry.

name: Hallucination
oneBreath: When the AI sounds sure but invents facts, quotes, or details that aren’t real.
does: Happen more when it lacks sources
doesNot: Not always intentional lying
Not solved by confidence alone
analogy: A student bluffing on an oral exam.
example: A fake book title or made-up citation.

name: RAG
oneBreath: The assistant looks up info from your files or the web, then answers using that — like an open-book test instead of guessing from memory.
doesNot: Not the same as retraining the model
Not a promise every answer is true
analogy: Open-book exam vs closed-book.
example: A company bot that searches the internal wiki first.

name: Chunking
oneBreath: Splitting long documents into smaller pieces so search and AI can handle them.
does: Fit big files into workable bites
doesNot: Not deleting content on purpose
Not one perfect split size for every doc
analogy: Cutting a book into chapters before shelving.
example: Break a 50-page PDF into short sections.

name: Vector database
oneBreath: A store built to find text by meaning — “what’s similar?” — not only exact keywords.
doesNot: Not a regular spreadsheet
Not the AI model itself
analogy: A library sorted by topic vibe, not just title A–Z.
example: Finding policy pages related to “parental leave.”

name: Retrieval
oneBreath: The step that fetches the most relevant snippets before the AI writes an answer.
doesNot: Not the writing step itself
Not always perfect relevance
analogy: A librarian fetching the best pages.
example: Top matching paragraphs for your question.

name: Reranking
oneBreath: A second pass that re-sorts search results so the best snippets rise to the top.
does: Improve what the AI actually reads
doesNot: Not a full rewrite of your documents
Not required for every tiny knowledge base
analogy: Resorting a messy stack after a quick grab.
example: Promote the paragraph that truly answers the ask.

name: Long context vs RAG
oneBreath: Two ways to give more info: paste a lot into the chat window, or fetch only what’s needed. Often you mix both.
does: Clarify when to paste vs search
Frame cost, speed, and freshness tradeoffs
doesNot: Not a claim one method always wins
Not the same as retraining
analogy: Carry the whole library vs ask for three books.
example: Paste a short spec; search a huge wiki with lookup.

name: Tool use / function calling
oneBreath: Letting the AI call outside helpers — search, calculators, APIs — instead of only writing text.
does: Take real actions in other systems
doesNot: Not unlimited control of your computer by default
Not safe without checks
analogy: Asking an assistant to use a calculator app.
example: Booking through an API from a chat.

name: Agent
oneBreath: An AI helper that plans steps, uses tools, and keeps going toward a goal — with some independence.
doesNot: Not a real person
Not always better than one clear prompt
analogy: An intern with a checklist and apps.
example: Research something, then file a ticket.

name: Multi-agent
oneBreath: Several specialized AI helpers working together — or checking each other — on one job.
does: Split roles like research and edit
doesNot: Not automatically smarter
Harder to debug when something goes wrong
analogy: A small team with different jobs.
example: One agent researches; another edits the draft.

name: Memory
oneBreath: Ways the system remembers facts across turns or visits — beyond what’s only on screen right now.
doesNot: Not the same as the short chat window alone
Raises privacy questions

nextStep.label: Compare to the short desk limit

analogy: A notebook the assistant keeps.
example: Remembering your name between sessions.

name: Orchestration
oneBreath: The control layer that sequences prompts, lookups, tools, and agents into a reliable workflow.
doesNot: Not the model’s brain weights
Can get overly complex
analogy: A stage manager for the show.
example: Workflow builders and agent graphs.

name: Skill
oneBreath: A reusable pack of instructions (and often tools) an agent can load to do one job well.
does: Specialize without retraining the whole model
doesNot: Not a human soft skill like teamwork
Not the same as fine-tuning

nextStep.label: See the safety cage around agents

analogy: A recipe card plus the utensils for one dish.
example: A “review this pull request” pack with steps and checks.
changing: Skills are becoming a portable way to share what agents can do.

name: Agent harness
oneBreath: The safety cage around an agent: permissions, loops, sandboxes, retries, and logs — separate from the model itself.
does: Limit what the agent can touch
Add rails and visibility around the loop
doesNot: Not the AI’s trained brain
Not a single prompt
analogy: A workshop bench with tools bolted down and a kill switch.
example: A coding agent stuck to one folder that logs every tool call.
changing: Good harness design matters as much as picking the model.

name: Human-in-the-loop
oneBreath: Keeping a person in the path — approve, edit, or stop — before risky actions go out.
doesNot: Not a reason to automate nothing
Not the same as training the model

nextStep.label: See the safety cage around agents

analogy: A co-pilot who still asks before landing.
example: Agent drafts a change; you click approve before it merges.

name: MCP
oneBreath: A shared plug standard so apps and agents can connect to tools and data without a custom hookup each time.
doesNot: Not a model by itself
Not required for every simple chatbot
analogy: USB for AI tools — one plug shape, many devices.
example: An editor agent connecting to GitHub and docs the same way.
changing: Quickly becoming common glue across agent products.

name: Evaluation
oneBreath: Measuring how well the AI or system works — with tests, graders, and real user signals.
doesNot: Not one universal score for everything
Not only vibes or gut feel
analogy: Exams for the assistant.
example: A fixed set of questions you re-run after each update.

name: Guardrails
oneBreath: Filters and rules that block or rewrite unsafe or off-policy outputs before users see them.
doesNot: Not perfect coverage
Not a replacement for good product design
analogy: Bouncers at the door of the reply.
example: Block requests for illegal how-tos.

name: Latency & cost
oneBreath: How long answers take and how much each call costs — the practical budget for using AI.
does: Force tradeoffs between quality and spend
Shape which model or steps you choose
doesNot: Not the same as answer quality
Not free just because it’s “in the cloud”
analogy: Taxi fare and travel time for each trip.
example: A cheaper small model for drafts; a bigger one for finals.

name: Safety / misuse
oneBreath: Risks of people using AI for harm — scams, abuse, or banned advice — and how products respond.
doesNot: Not solved by one filter forever
Not only a technical problem
analogy: Rules for a powerful tool in public hands.
example: Blocking help for phishing emails.

name: Observability / tracing
oneBreath: Recording prompts, tool calls, timing, and results so you can see why a system did what it did.
does: Track cost and speed in real use
doesNot: Not the same as grading answer quality
Not a substitute for safety rails
analogy: A flight recorder for the assistant.
example: A timeline of each tool call when a task fails.
